task.name: The seam #2399 built has never been used, so every sprint-lifecycle responsibility still lives in one module and unrelated sprint changes still collide on it
task.story_text:
## Why

#2325 and #2399 built an extraction seam and nothing has moved through it. `run_sprint` takes one
run context, the execution state owns what the frame held, five named lifecycle functions are at
module scope, and structural tests fail if frame capture or member-passing returns. All of that is
real. None of it has been used.

The consequence is that the seam's value is still unproven. Forge claims **files**, not functions, so
sprint-lifecycle responsibilities that all live in one 7,777-line module still produce one collision
claim: two stories changing unrelated parts of a sprint run still serialise against each other, and a
reviewer of either still loads the same module. Moving a responsibility out is the first action that
tests whether the seam does what it was built to do, and the first that changes anything a story can
observe.

The seam is demonstrably usable. #2349 produced the pattern to follow: it moved routing evidence into
its own module, and that module imports nothing from the module it came from — not a relocation with
a dependency left behind, but an actual separation.

The responsibility to move first is **sprint audit publication**. It is the largest cohesive group
already at module scope — roughly 370 lines across five functions — it is reached from only two
places in the runner, it already carries its own error type, and it is the group least entangled
with sprint orchestration state, since its work is against git and the filesystem rather than
against the run in progress. Naming it here is deliberate: left to selection at implementation time,
the cheapest cluster gets chosen rather than the most useful boundary, which is the same substitution
ADR-0008 Amendment 3 recorded when a blocked story relocated 413 lines to whichever module was
cheapest.

The remaining responsibilities are separate issues, filed once this one has shown what a move costs
and what it breaks.

## Example

The observable outcome is a collision that stops happening. Today a story changing how a sprint
publishes its audits and a story changing how it resolves a queued pull request both claim the sprint
runner, so the scheduler serialises them however unrelated their changes are:

```
today
  story A  (audit publishing)     claims  sprint runner module
  story B  (queued PR resolution) claims  sprint runner module
  -> scheduler serialises B behind A

after one responsibility moves
  story A  claims  the moved module
  story B  claims  sprint runner module
  -> A and B run in parallel
```

The second observable outcome is that the moved responsibility can be exercised on its own: a test
constructs what it needs and calls it, with no sprint running, no worktree, and no agent invoked.

## Acceptance criteria

- Sprint audit publication is moved out of the sprint runner into its own module. The responsibility
  begins with constructing the terminal sprint audit and summary inputs and ends with publishing the
  canonical run artifacts and reporting a publication failure. Everything inside that boundary moves;
  a move leaving part of it behind does not satisfy this. Imports and call sites elsewhere change as
  a consequence of the move, which is expected — what may not change is any other responsibility's
  behaviour or ownership.
- The new module does not import the sprint runner. Separation is what makes the move worth doing; a
  module that still depends on the one it left is a relocation.
- No moved function captures state from an enclosing frame, and none receives individually threaded
  members of the execution state. A moved function receives the execution state, the run context, or
  its own per-call arguments.
- The moved responsibility has tests that call it directly and assert on what it returns and what it
  writes, constructing what it needs rather than running a sprint.
- The sprint runner claims one fewer responsibility afterwards, and no other responsibility is
  partially moved by this change.
- Sprint behaviour is unchanged: for the same inputs a run executes the same stories in the same
  batches and writes the same outcomes, costs and audit fields as before the move.

## Already satisfied — do not redo

The run context, execution state, cost ledger and stop condition exist and own their state; the five
named lifecycle functions are at module scope; structural tests added by #2399 guard all of it. A
change reopening any of those ownership decisions is out of scope, and no further preparatory work is
needed before a responsibility can move.

## Out of scope

The remaining sprint-lifecycle responsibilities. They are separate issues rather than a checklist
here, because the point of doing one first is to learn what a move costs before committing to the
rest. Also out of scope: reducing any module below `max_module_lines` — this milestone is judged on
independent changeability, and making module size the scoreboard rebuilds the withdrawn ADR-0008
ratchet at milestone scale.

Note that ADR-0008's 2026-08-08 amendment records module size as the smaller of two cost factors,
with per-story change size the larger and unaddressed by this work.

handoff.summary: Moved sprint audit publication out of sprint/runner.py into a new sprint/audit_publish.py. The new module owns the responsibility end to end: it derives the terminal audit and summary inputs (ref→slug map, canonical refs, tasks-by-slug, triage actions) from the run context, calls the writers in audit.py, generates the sprint RCA, and then commits, pushes, verifies and reports on the canonical per-run audit JSON — carrying StoryRunAuditPublishError, the AUDIT_PUBLISH_* end states, and the four publish helpers with it. run_sprint now makes two calls, write_terminal_sprint_audits(_sprint_state, ...) and publish_story_run_audits(_sprint_state, lands_locally=...), each taking the execution state rather than threaded members. The module imports audit.py's writers and coordinator workspace/util, never the runner; a structural test in tests/test_sprint_audit_publish.py parses the module and fails on any import of sprint.runner, including a TYPE_CHECKING or function-local one. Because the state types live in runner.py, the two entry points annotate the state as Any with the contract documented in the module docstring and sprint/CONVENTIONS.md. Added SprintRunContext.slug_by_canonical_ref so the audit writers and the post-sprint hook share one derivation instead of duplicating it. runner.py went from 8006 to 7664 lines; audit_publish.py is 455.

soft: Coordinator is pure Python — no LLM calls for routing or process decisions
Schema validation is the integrity boundary — do not relax cross-validation rules

Keep modules single-purpose. Extract when a responsibility separates from its neighbours — never to satisfy a line count. Putting a change in an already-large module is correct if that is where it belongs; a module carved at whatever line got the count down is worse than the large module it came from.
Keep pure-data types in low-dependency modules with stdlib-only imports
Separate prompt construction, output parsing, and coordinator control flow

When adding or modifying data that flows between coordinator phases, instrument the change so the actual values are visible in the audit trail — diagnosing sprint failures requires tracing real data, not reconstructing it
Do not create files outside src/, tests/, or docs/. If you need a scratch file for exploration, delete it before committing.

Changes that affect coordinator phase boundaries, state handoff between phases, or adaptive routing/config propagation must include seam-level integration tests covering the touched boundary. Unit tests alone are insufficient when correctness depends on cross-phase state flow.

reviewer_tier.rationale: 2 buckets — planning quality is bimodal: mid planner for mechanical stories (1-5), strong planner for design-heavy ones (6-10)

reviewer_count.rationale: 3 buckets — min reviewers for low-risk (1-4), configured midpoint for medium (5-7), max for high-risk (8-10), bounded by min_reviewers/max_reviewers

final.rationale: [preflight] 3 reviewer(s), tier strong, providers ['openai', 'anthropic', 'google'], complexity score 8; per-story routing cost target: unset
